query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Refining the dispersion of fine precipitates in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy through a controlled heat treatment improves high-temperature wear resistance and reduces localized plastic deformation by hindering dislocation motion during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline coating with a uniform solid solution or coarse precipitate distribution without deliberate modification.
generation.intervention: Subject the coating to a controlled heat treatment designed to refine precipitate size and increase their volume fraction.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (approximately 600–800°C) under comparable applied loads and sliding speeds.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined dispersion of fine precipitates within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The fine precipitates serve as obstacles to dislocation motion and dynamic plastic deformation during sliding, thereby decreasing localized softening and wear by impeding plastic flow and crack initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the heat-treated coating should exhibit a lower wear rate and reduced indicators of microscopic plastic deformation (e.g., fewer slip bands, reduced micro-crack formation) under high-temperature sliding.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating in its as-deposited state with a coarser or less-distributed precipitate arrangement.
generation.boundary: These effects are predicted to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (600–800°C); behavior at lower temperatures or under non-sliding conditions may differ.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvements in wear rate and deformation reduction remain to be determined, and other microstructural features (such as grain size effects) might also influence the results.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings: one in the baseline state and one subjected to the controlled heat treatment to refine precipitates. Conduct identical sliding wear tests at 600–800°C under the same load and speed conditions.
measurements: Wear loss (e.g., volume or mass loss) quantification
Microscopic evaluation (SEM/TEM) of precipitate distribution and signs of plastic deformation
Hardness measurements before and after sliding
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and/or does not exhibit evidence of reduced localized deformation (e.g., comparable dislocation structures or crack initiation) compared to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: At the beginning of the 21st century, Yeh [] and Cantor [] first proposed the concept of a multi-principal element alloy, that is, a solid solution formed by mixing five or more elements according to a certain molar ratio (the atomic percentage of each element is between 5% and 35%), and defined it as a high-entropy alloy (HEA). HEAs have been shown to have a variety of outstanding properties, such as high strength values, high hardness values, and excellent corrosion resistance and wear resistance [,,,,,,,,,], leading to extensive research and development as well as high application potential. More specifically, HEAs are expected to be applied as high temperature-resistant alloys, wear-resistant alloys and corrosion-resistant alloys, etc. Unlike conventional alloys, which are generally composed of one or two primary elements, HEAs possess a plethora of unique characteristics that place them at the central region of the phase diagram. Due to their extensive alloy composition space and wide-ranging microstructure possibilities, HEAs exhibit remarkable potential for use in the field of friction materials [,,,,,,,,].

As can be seen from Figure 12b,c, compared with the substrate sample, there was no visible crack found in the wear area of the LC(FeCoNiCr) and LC(CoCrNi) samples, and the delamination and grooves were obviously alleviated. Moreover, the size of the wear debris decreased. The reason for the wear resistance improvement of the untreated coating samples was the high surface hardness. A hard surface could hinder the deformation of the material, reducing micro-cracks as well as weakening the delamination wear. It can be found from Figure 12d,e that the wear of the two UB-treated coating samples was greatly weakened and the quantity and volume of wear debris in the wear areas decreased, and the grooves were shallowed compared with their corresponding untreated coating samples. The grains of the two UB-treated coating samples were refined via UB treatment, and their hardness and yield strengths were significantly improved. Thereby, the volume and quantity of wear debris produced in the wear test were reduced, and the abrasive wear was alleviated [,].

frame.goal: To understand and improve overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior under sliding in high-temperature conditions by identifying and manipulating a key microstructural feature.
frame.limitation: Current uncertainty exists regarding which microstructural mechanism governs wear resistance and localized plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding, limiting predictive control over service life.
